analysis.one_liner: Bans public companies from buying back their own shares and requires worker-elected board seats.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Reward Work Act would have done two things. First, it would prohibit publicly traded companies from buying back their own stock on the open market — the practice known as a stock buyback, where a company uses its cash to purchase its own shares, which pushes the share price up and mostly benefits big shareholders and executives whose pay is tied to stock prices. Second, it would require every public company to let its employees elect one-third of the board of directors, by a one-worker-one-vote election, within two years. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, rank-and-file employees at public companies would gain board representation and a direct voice in major corporate decisions. Workers more broadly could gain if companies shifted cash away from buybacks and toward wages, hiring, or investment, which is the bill's stated premise. Small long-term shareholders would also benefit relative to large institutional sellers, since buybacks currently channel corporate cash to whoever sells shares.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any public company issuer from purchasing its own equity securities on a national securities exchange, and voids the SEC safe-harbor rule (Rule 10b-18) that currently shields buybacks from manipulation claims.

Amends the Securities Exchange Act so no company may register its securities on a national exchange unless at least one-third of its directors are chosen by employees in a one-employee-one-vote election, with the SEC and NLRB writing rules to make those elections fair and phased in within two years.

Preserves tender offers (direct offers to buy shares from holders) as the only lawful route for a company to repurchase its own stock, so buybacks are not banned outright but moved off the open market.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies and their large shareholders would bear the cost: the loss of open-market buybacks as a tool for returning cash and supporting the share price, and the addition of worker-elected directors who answer to employees rather than to investors alone. Executives whose compensation is tied to stock price would lose a mechanism that reliably lifts it.

drawbacks.text: Companies could still repurchase shares through tender offers under the bill's own carve-out, so the prohibition is partial — a company willing to run a tender offer can keep buying back stock, and wealthy holders with shares to sell may capture more of the benefit than rank-and-file employees ever would.

A genuine economic objection: buybacks return capital to investors who can redeploy it elsewhere, and blocking them could reduce returns for the roughly half of households that own stock through retirement accounts, while doing nothing to force companies to raise wages instead.

Requiring one-third of boards to be employee-elected would be a major change to corporate governance for every listed company, and opponents would argue it raises costs and creates divided boards without proof it improves company performance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a real and debated problem — trillions of dollars in buybacks that critics say go to shareholders instead of workers — but it is a blunt instrument. It does not require companies to spend the money on wages, it leaves a tender-offer loophole, and the worker-board mandate applies to every listed company at once. The upside for workers is indirect and unproven; the compliance burden on companies is direct and certain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Chuy Garcia introduced the Reward Work Act in the House on May 25, 2023, joined by an initial list of fellow House Democrats including Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Barbara Lee, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Katie Porter.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever recorded.
It ultimately attracted 32 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public companies and their large shareholders are better off, because open-market buybacks and investor-controlled boards remain fully lawful and untouched. No worker board representation was created.

for.name: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Reward Work Act on May 25, 2023.

for.name: 32 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican-chaired in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 19 months of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and committee agendas
against.what_they_did: Controlled which bills got committee time and floor votes; the bill, sponsored only by Democrats, never advanced past referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: The bill would end open-market buybacks, a tool companies use to lift their share price, and would seat worker-elected directors on their boards. Executives whose pay depends on stock price would lose the most, which is why the corporate lobby opposes such bans.

industries.industry: Large institutional shareholders and asset managers
industries.note: Buybacks return corporate cash to whoever sells shares, and big institutions are the biggest sellers; ending them reduces a reliable source of share-price gains. Some retiree investors with index funds would also see somewhat lower returns.

industries.industry: Wall Street exchanges and trading firms
industries.note: A ban on issuer purchases would eliminate a large, steady block of buy-side volume from national exchanges and the brokers and market makers that execute it.
